questions.problem: Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{24}∼N(5,{12}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $n=24$ from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}?$
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=24,\,\mu =5,\,\sigma =12.
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(5,\frac{{12}^{2}}{24}) \\  & ∼N(5,6).\end{aligned}
$$

If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(7,\frac{{14}^{2}}{49}) \\  & ∼N(7,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5) & =P(\frac{6.8-7}{\sqrt{4}}<Z<\frac{7.5-7}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =P(-0.1<Z<0.25) \\  & =Φ(0.25)-Φ(-0.1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.25)=0.5987,\end{aligned}
$$

and by the symmetry of the normal distribution,

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.1) & =1-Φ(0.1) \\  & =1-0.5398 \\  & =0.4602.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5) & =Φ(0.25)-Φ(-0.1) \\  & =0.5987-0.4602 \\  & =0.1385.\end{aligned}
$$

If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(4,\frac{{18}^{2}}{36}) \\  & ∼N(4,9).\end{aligned}

We're required to find $P(|\overset{―}{X}|<2.07).$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|<2.07) & =P(-2.07<\overset{―}{X}<2.07) \\  & =P(\frac{-2.07-4}{\sqrt{9}}<Z<\frac{2.07-4}{\sqrt{9}}) \\  & =P(-2.02<Z<-0.64) \\  & =Φ(-0.64)-Φ(-2.02)\end{aligned}

If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-14,\frac{{16}^{2}}{64}) \\  & ∼N(-14,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>-14.86).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>-14.86) & =P(Z>\frac{-14.86-(-14)}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =P(Z>-0.43).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the complement of the normal distribution, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>-0.43) & =1-P(Z\le -0.43) \\  & =1-Φ(-0.43).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.43)=0.3336.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>-14.86) & =1-Φ(-0.43) \\  & =1-0.3336 \\  & =0.6664.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-3,\frac{{8}^{2}}{16}) \\  & ∼N(-3,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.5).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.5) & =1-P(|\overset{―}{X}|<0.5) \\  & =1-P(-0.5<\overset{―}{X}<0.5) \\  & =1-P(\frac{-0.5-(-3)}{\sqrt{4}}<Z<\frac{0.5-(-3)}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =1-P(1.25<Z<1.75) \\  & =1-(Φ(1.75)-Φ(1.25)) \\  & =1+Φ(1.25)-Φ(1.75)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.25) & =0.8944, \\ Φ(1.75) & =0.9599.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.5) & =1+Φ(1.25)-Φ(1.75) \\  & =1+0.8944-0.9599 \\  & =0.9345.\end{aligned}
$$

then the sample mean $\overline{X}$ has the distribution

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
X_i\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad 1\leq i\leq n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overline{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu=75,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma = 10,$ and that the sample size $n=10.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(75,\frac{{10}^{2}}{10}) \\  & ∼N(75,10).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P( \overline{X} \lt 70).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<70) & =P(Z<\frac{70-75}{\sqrt{10}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-1.58) \\  & =Φ(-1.58)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.58) & =0.0571.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<70) & =Φ(-1.58) \\  & =0.0571.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ be a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a normal population $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2.$ In other words,   

$$
X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n} \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2).
$$

In this case, we can easily determine the sampling distribution of the sample mean

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n X_i.
$$

Recall the following:

- The sum of $n$ independent and identically distributed normal random variables is normally distributed. Thus, 

$$
Y = \displaystyle \sum\limits_{i=1}^n X_i
$$

is normally distributed.

- A normally distributed random variable scaled by a constant factor is normally distributed. Thus, 

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac1n\cdot Y
$$

is normally distributed.

Also, we previously saw that the expected value of the sample mean equals the population mean, i.e., 

$$
\textrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mu,
$$

and the variance of the sample mean is

$$
\textrm{Var}[\overline{X}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}.
$$

Putting all of this together, we obtain that

$$
\overline{X} \sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right),
$$

In other words, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and variance $\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}.$
